name: Web & Browser Security
description: Attacks and defenses for the web platform: browsers, JavaScript, the DOM, web apps, and server-side web code.

ccs.narrative:
Web security at CCS has tracked the browser as an expanding attack surface, from script-based tracking to regulatory compliance. The 2018 cohort exposed the browser as an unwilling participant in emerging abuses: MineSweeper: An In-depth Look into Drive-by Cryptocurrency Mining and Its Defense (CCS 2018) and How You Get Shot in the Back: A Systematical Study about Cryptojacking in the Real World (CCS 2018) together documented cryptojacking as a novel browser-native monetization abuse. Mystique: Uncovering Information Leakage from Browser Extensions (CCS 2018) showed that the extension permission model leaks user data broadly, and The Web's Sixth Sense: A Study of Scripts Accessing Smartphone Sensors (CCS 2018) exposed mobile sensor data as a tracking vector.

GDPR compliance became a research topic immediately after the regulation took effect: (Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field (CCS 2019) was the defining empirical work, measuring dark patterns across thousands of sites. DECO: Liberating Web Data Using Decentralized Oracles for TLS (CCS 2020) repurposed the TLS handshake to let users prove data provenance to third parties.

Authentication and authorization auditing matured into automated tools. The Cookie Hunter: Automated Black-box Auditing for Web Authentication and Authorization Flaws (CCS 2020) automatically discovered account-access bugs in live web applications. Phishing detection extended into blockchain contexts with TxPhishScope: Towards Detecting and Understanding Transaction-based Phishing on Ethereum (CCS 2023).

milestones.note: Characterized browser-based cryptomining as a distinct threat and built a robust behavioral detector.

ndss.narrative:
Web and browser security at NDSS has been defined by two persistent themes: the exploitation of dynamic scripting engines and the arms race over content-security policies and cross-origin isolation. SYNODE (NDSS 2018) automatically prevented injection attacks in Node.js by analyzing and hardening module interactions at the AST level. CodeAlchemist (NDSS 2019) used semantics-aware code-brick reassembly to fuzz JavaScript engines for memory bugs, a technique that complemented grammar-based approaches like NAUTILUS.

Content Security Policy measurement (Complex Security Policy?, NDSS 2020) documented how CSP deployments fail in practice: most policies are too permissive to block real attacks. DRAWN APART (NDSS 2022) showed that browser-based GPU fingerprinting is a durable tracking mechanism that survives private browsing modes, while Favocado (NDSS 2021) targeted the binding layer between JavaScript and native browser APIs—a previously under-fuzzed interface.

FUZZILLI (NDSS 2023) became the most-cited recent paper in this topic by delivering a coverage-guided fuzzer purpose-built for JavaScript JIT compilers, finding numerous CVEs in V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore. BreakSPF (NDSS 2024) then pivoted to email authentication, showing how shared cloud infrastructure undermines SPF verification. YuraScanner (NDSS 2025) closed the loop by using LLMs to drive task-oriented web application scanning, extending automated web vulnerability discovery to business-logic flaws that syntax-based tools miss.

milestones.title: SYNODE: Understanding and Automatically Preventing Injection Attacks on NODE.JS
milestones.note: SYNODE analyzes and automatically mitigates injection vulnerabilities in Node.js modules using static analysis and runtime policies.

milestones.title: CodeAlchemist: Semantics-Aware Code Generation to Find Vulnerabilities in JavaScript Engines
milestones.note: Generates semantically valid JavaScript via code bricks to fuzz and find vulnerabilities in JavaScript engines.

milestones.title: Complex Security Policy? A Longitudinal Analysis of Deployed Content Security Policies
milestones.note: This longitudinal study analyzes deployed Content Security Policies using Internet Archive data to assess their effectiveness against script injection

milestones.title: Favocado: Fuzzing the Binding Code of JavaScript Engines Using Semantically Correct Test Cases
milestones.note: Fuzzes JavaScript engine binding layers using semantically correct test cases to find memory bugs.

milestones.title: DRAWN APART: A Device Identification Technique based on Remote GPU Fingerprinting
milestones.note: Fingerprints devices by remotely measuring GPU characteristics via browser scripts to identify and track users.

milestones.title: FUZZILLI: Fuzzing for JavaScript JIT Compiler Vulnerabilities
milestones.note: FUZZILLI is a coverage-guided fuzzer generating semantically valid JavaScript to discover JIT compiler vulnerabilities in browser engines.

milestones.title: BreakSPF: How Shared Infrastructures Magnify SPF Vulnerabilities Across the Internet
milestones.note: BreakSPF shows how shared infrastructures magnify SPF vulnerabilities, enabling large-scale email spoofing across the Internet.

milestones.title: YuraScanner: Leveraging LLMs for Task-driven Web App Scanning
milestones.note: Leverages LLMs to drive task-oriented automated scanning of web applications for vulnerabilities.

sp.narrative:
Web security at IEEE S&P spans browser fingerprinting, tracking, web API vulnerabilities, and browser extension security. The 2018 cohort addressed tracking and PII exposure: FP-STALKER: Tracking Browser Fingerprint Evolutions (S&P 2018) showed that fingerprints persist across browser updates well enough for long-term user tracking, while Privacy Risks with Facebook's PII-Based Targeting (S&P 2018) audited how data brokers use personal information to micro-target advertising audiences.

The 2019-2020 period expanded to phishing measurement and browser extension security. PhishFarm: A Scalable Framework for Measuring the Effectiveness of Evasion Techniques against Browser Phishing Blacklists (S&P 2019) measured how long phishing sites survive detection by deploying controlled bait sites against real browser blacklists. EmPoWeb: Empowering Web Applications with Browser Extensions (S&P 2019) exposed how extensions grant web apps capabilities beyond the browser security model. Fuzzing JavaScript Engines with Aspect-preserving Mutation (S&P 2020) brought greybox fuzzing to JS engine bugs.

From 2021, detection and measurement matured. Fingerprinting the Fingerprinters: Learning to Detect Browser Fingerprinting Behaviors (S&P 2021) inverted the problem—using ML to identify scripts that collect fingerprints. AdGraph: A Graph-Based Approach to Ad and Tracker Blocking (S&P 2020) demonstrated graph-based tracker detection outperforming filter lists. Black Widow: Blackbox Data-driven Web Scanning (S&P 2021) introduced purely blackbox scanning for stored XSS and CSRF vulnerabilities.

By 2023-2025, LLM-generated phishing pages and deepfake-assisted social engineering entered the S&P web-security agenda, while formal analysis of web standards (OAuth, OpenID) continued to find protocol-level flaws in widely deployed identity infrastructure.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from USENIX Security 2018, reflect a web-security field grappling with the consequences of a maturing, JavaScript-heavy platform on both client and server. Several attacked the new server-side reality of Node.js: "Freezing the Web: A Study of ReDoS Vulnerabilities in JavaScript-based Web Servers" (USENIX 2018) and "A Sense of Time for JavaScript and Node.js" (USENIX 2018) showed that a single-threaded event loop made algorithmic-complexity and event-handler-poisoning denial of service unusually easy, a theme echoed by "Rampart: Protecting Web Applications from CPU-Exhaustion Denial-of-Service Attacks" (USENIX 2018). In parallel, classic web-app and protocol weaknesses were being attacked at scale and with automation: "NAVEX" (USENIX 2018) generated exploits for dynamic web apps, while "Efail" (USENIX 2018) and the SSO and third-party-cookie studies ("O Single Sign-Off", "Who Left Open the Cookie Jar?", USENIX 2018) exposed how composed real-world systems — email encryption, federated login, cookie policies — break at their seams. A privacy thread also opened here with "Fp-Scanner" (USENIX 2018) on browser fingerprinting.

By 2019-2020 the field shifted toward systematic defenses and toward treating the browser itself as the security boundary. "Site Isolation: Process Separation for Web Sites within the Browser" (USENIX 2019) was a landmark, putting each site in its own process to contain renderer compromise and side channels — arguably the most consequential architectural defense of the period. Reduction-of-attack-surface thinking appeared in "Less is More: Quantifying the Security Benefits of Debloating Web Applications" (USENIX 2019). The platform also kept expanding, and so did its risks: "Everything Old is New Again: Binary Security of WebAssembly" (USENIX 2020) showed that Wasm reintroduced memory-corruption hazards the web thought it had left behind, while "Montage" (USENIX 2020) advanced neural-network-guided fuzzing of JavaScript engines, signaling the rise of automated bug-finding for browser internals.

The 2021 papers crystallized the realization that the browser is a hardware side-channel surface. "SMASH: Synchronized Many-sided Rowhammer Attacks from JavaScript" (USENIX 2021) and "Prime+Probe 1, JavaScript 0" (USENIX 2021) ran microarchitectural attacks straight from a web page, and "Swivel: Hardening WebAssembly against Spectre" (USENIX 2021) responded by hardening Wasm against Spectre. Alongside this, web-app analysis grew more sophisticated with graph-based program analysis — "JAW" (USENIX 2021) for client-side CSRF and, the next year, "Mining Node.js Vulnerabilities via Object Dependence Graph and Query" (USENIX 2022) and "FUGIO" (USENIX 2022) for PHP object injection. Fingerprinting research matured into a cat-and-mouse around extensions ("Fingerprinting in Style", USENIX 2021).

Most recently the area has split along several mature fronts: privacy-and-policy compliance at web scale ("Automating Cookie Consent and GDPR Violation Detection" and "Leaky Forms", USENIX 2022), deep-learning-based ecosystem defense ("Inferring Phishing Intention via Webpage Appearance and Dynamics", USENIX 2022), the security of blended mobile/web runtimes ("Identity Confusion in WebView-based Mobile App-in-app Ecosystems", USENIX 2022), and increasingly powerful automated bug discovery — "FuzzJIT" (USENIX 2023) targeting JIT compilers and "Atropos" (USENIX 2024) fuzzing server-side PHP web apps. The throughline is clear: what began as point studies of specific bugs has evolved into architectural isolation, hardware-aware threat models, graph-based static analysis, and automated, learning-guided discovery across the full web stack.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers here (2018) capture a web platform under pressure on several distinct fronts at once. One cluster is about abuse of the browser as a compute engine: drive-by cryptomining surfaced as a real threat, studied in depth by MineSweeper (CCS 2018) and measured in the wild by How You Get Shot in the Back (CCS 2018). A second cluster targets the server side and the JavaScript code now running there, where algorithmic-complexity and injection bugs became first-class web threats — Freezing the Web (USENIX 2018) on ReDoS, SYNODE (NDSS 2018) on Node.js injection, NAVEX (USENIX 2018) on automated exploit generation, and Rampart (USENIX 2018) on CPU-exhaustion DoS. A third, very active cluster is privacy and tracking: FP-STALKER (S&P 2018) showed browser fingerprints evolve but stay trackable, while Mystique (CCS 2018) and The Web's Sixth Sense (CCS 2018) exposed leakage through extensions and device sensors. Classic web-app flaws also got fresh, automated treatment, notably DOM-based XSS in Riding out DOMsday (NDSS 2018).

The 2019 work marks a regulatory and architectural shift. With GDPR in force, measurement of consent and tracking moved center stage — (Un)informed Consent (CCS 2019) and Oh, the Places You've Been! (CCS 2019) turned privacy into a compliance-and-transparency question. On defense, the browser itself was re-architected: Site Isolation (USENIX 2019) brought per-site process separation to production browsers, and Less is More (USENIX 2019) pushed debloating as attack-surface reduction. Meanwhile JavaScript-engine security matured into a fuzzing discipline with CodeAlchemist (NDSS 2019), and the cat-and-mouse with ML detectors began, as HideNoSeek (CCS 2019) camouflaged malicious scripts inside benign ASTs.

By 2020-2021 two themes dominate. First, the GDPR/consent measurement line hardens into legal-compliance auditing — Do Cookie Banners Respect my Choice? (S&P 2020) and later Automating Cookie Consent and GDPR Violation Detection (USENIX 2022) — paired with smarter, learning-based anti-tracking such as AdGraph (S&P 2020) and Fingerprinting the Fingerprinters (S&P 2021). Second, engine and low-level security explodes: JS-engine fuzzing advances through aspect-preserving mutation (S&P 2020), neural-guided Montage (USENIX 2020), and differential JIT-Picking (CCS 2022), while WebAssembly becomes a security object in its own right — Everything Old is New Again (USENIX 2020) on Wasm binary security and Swivel (USENIX 2021) on hardening Wasm against Spectre.

The most recent frontier is the browser as a hardware attack surface and the persistence of social-engineering threats. SMASH (USENIX 2021) drove Rowhammer from JavaScript and Prime+Probe 1, JavaScript 0 (USENIX 2021) defeated browser side-channel defenses, collapsing the gap between web code and microarchitectural exploitation. In parallel, phishing detection moved toward learning-based, vision-driven approaches (PhishFarm, S&P 2019; Inferring Phishing Intention, USENIX 2022). Taken together, the area has evolved from auditing web-app and tracking abuses toward defending an enormously broad stack — from consent banners and JS engines down to Wasm sandboxes and the CPU caches the browser runs on.
